_comment: Golden canon frames: what an epoch-1 client puts on the wire, and what
Starling's services must read back. Checked in as bytes rather than
generated at test time, deliberately, a fixture both sides build from
their own encoder agrees with itself while disagreeing with the wire,
which is exactly the failure D1 was.
Each entry is one complete frame: type:u16 BE, len:u32 BE, payload.
The client asserts it *produces* these; Starling asserts it *consumes*
them. Either side drifting fails on its own side, with a name.
A frame only belongs here if its bytes are the same everywhere. Push
registration is the counter-example and the reason this is written down:
the client fills `platform` from std::env::consts::OS, so the frame it
produces on Windows is not the one it produces in CI. That is fine on the
wire and fatal in a fixture.
Regenerate only when the canon deliberately changes, and update both
sides in the same commit, see PROTOCOL-MIGRATION.md M6.

frames.name: social: thumbs-up reaction on message m-1 in channel 4
frames.means: SocialEnvelope{ Reaction{ channel: 4, message_id: 'm-1', unicode emoji } }

frames.name: social: a poll with two options in channel 4
frames.means: SocialEnvelope{ Poll{ poll_id: 'p-1', channel: 4, question: 'lunch?', options: ['yes', 'no'] } }

frames.name: pchat: an encrypted message in channel 4
frames.means: PchatEnvelope{ Message{ message_id: 'm-7', channel: 4, ciphertext: deadbeef, sent_at_ms: 1700000000000, epoch: 2, chain_index: 9, sender_cert: empty } }

frames.name: pchat: fetch the last 50 messages of channel 4
frames.means: PchatEnvelope{ Fetch{ channel: 4, page: Cursor{ limit: 50 } } }
